1.goal: To open the lesson that closes the block, and to have her name what she can already say at a desk.
run: Read the question on screen with her: she is at the hotel desk again — what does she already know how to say?
Take whatever comes, in any order. Write it down.
Then say in one sentence what today is: the whole check-in, from good morning to thank you.
Read the records of the three previous lessons before the lesson starts — the next block is planned from them.
exact: What today is: "Today you do the whole check-in. From good morning to thank you."
1.expected: Two or three things she can name: her name, the dates, asking for a repeat. What she leaves out is as useful as what she says.
1.support: If nothing comes, name lesson 1 and let her find the four sentences herself.
1.challenge: Ask her which of the three lessons she thinks she will use most today.
1.monitoring: What she claims she can do, before doing it. It is compared with the attempt on screen 3.
1.evidence: Her own list of what she can say. Half a minute, and it is the before of this lesson.
1.transition: Move on when she has named at least two things.

2.goal: To place the scene of the whole lesson: she arrives, the desk asks, she answers, and at some point she asks for something.
run: Read the scene with her. The Portuguese is under it.
Confirm: she arrives, the desk asks, she answers — and at some point she asks for one thing.
Do not mention the question that comes at the end of round one.
2.expected: She can say what she is about to do, in one sentence.
2.support: If she is unsure what asking for one thing means, name one example she already has: a room with a window.
2.challenge: Ask what she would want to ask for at a real hotel.
2.monitoring: Whether she treats the request as part of the check-in or as an extra.
2.evidence: What she says she would ask for. It becomes the content of screen 7.
2.transition: Move on when she knows what she is about to do.

3.goal: The whole check-in with no model. This attempt is half of today's evidence.
3.interaction: Role-play. You are Emma at the desk.
run: Nothing on screen. Open the desk and wait.
Let the attempt run without correcting or suggesting. If she stops for a long moment, give the first word of the sentence and only that.
Write down four things: did she greet? did she say her name? did she confirm the dates? did she ask for anything?
exact: Opening, as Emma: "Good afternoon! Checking in?"
If she stops for a long moment, the first word and only that: "My…" / "I have…" / "Two…"
3.expected: An incomplete check-in. The greeting and the request are the two that usually go missing, and that is what screens 4 and 6 exist for.
3.support: The first word of the sentence, and nothing more. Do not finish it and do not rephrase it.
3.challenge: Say nothing after her first sentence and let the silence ask the next question.
3.monitoring: The four items above, and how long each silence lasts.
3.evidence: The unmodeled attempt: which of the four moments she produced on her own. Half of today's evidence, taken before any input.
3.transition: Move on when she has finished, even with half of it missing.

4.goal: To show the three moments of a check-in, after her own attempt.
run: She places the six lines and checks. Go through the result with her.
Talk only about the ones she got wrong.
CCQ: what costs two words and changes the whole tone? (Good morning and thank you.)
If she skipped the greeting on screen 3, this is where it comes up, without making a point of it.
4.expected: Six placed. The two closing lines are the ones that get discussed.
4.support: If a line is hard to place, ask when she would say it: on the way in, or on the way out.
4.challenge: Ask her to add one line of her own to each of the three moments.
4.monitoring: Whether she notices on her own that she skipped the greeting.
4.evidence: Whether the missing move becomes visible to her once the shape is on screen.
4.transition: Move on when the six are in place.

5.goal: For her to see that she already has the three moves for a question she was not expecting.
run: She marks the three that keep the conversation going and checks.
Then ask where those sentences came from. (Lesson 2.)
Let her be the one to say that she already has what she needs.
5.expected: In her own words: this is not new content — she has had it since lesson 2.
5.support: If she does not make the connection, name lesson 2 and let her find the two sentences herself.
5.challenge: Ask which of the three she would use for a question she did not understand at all.
5.monitoring: Whether she recognizes her own repertoire, or treats every screen as new material.
5.evidence: Whether she can name where a sentence came from. It is the difference between collecting phrases and having a repertoire.
5.transition: Move on when she has recognized the three.

6.goal: To make one opening automatic — Can I have…? — and to keep the two repair sentences warm.
6.interaction: S says the sentences aloud; then T gives two new things to ask for.
run: She says the five sentences on screen out loud, one at a time.
Then give her two things that are NOT on the screen, and let her build the request with the same opening.
Correct in one word and move on. After this screen there is no more correcting until the feedback.
exact: The two extra things, one at a time: "A taxi on Saturday." / "A late check-out."
The correction, in one word, then straight on: "Can I have."
6.expected: The five sentences said out loud, and two new requests built with Can I have…?
6.support: Give the opening — Can I… — and let her finish.
6.challenge: Ask for a third thing of her own that is not on the list.
6.monitoring: Whether the opening comes as one block, or is rebuilt word by word each time.
6.evidence: Whether Can I have…? has become one block.
6.transition: Move on when the two extra requests have come out.

7.goal: The whole check-in, with one question nobody showed her.
7.interaction: Role-play. You are Emma at the desk; the second voice comes from the recording.
run: Run the check-in as Emma. Keep the audio panel closed until you need it.
When she is nearly closing, open Audio and play the recording once — it is Rui, with the taxi question.
If she asks for a repeat, play it again and count it as a success: it is the move from lesson 2, and it is what this cycle measures.
If she answers only yes or no, that is correct. It is a yes-or-no question.
Do not correct during. Write down what she says, as she says it.
exact: Opening, as Emma: "Good afternoon! Welcome to Hotel Marina."
When she asks for a repeat: "Of course." — and play it again, with nothing added.
If she stops after the question, hand the turn back: "So — Saturday. Is that a yes?"
7.expected: The four moments, and a yes or a no to the taxi question — with or without a repeat first.
7.support: Play it again. That is the whole support, and asking for it is the point.
7.challenge: Ask a second unexpected question yourself, this one about breakfast times.
7.monitoring: Whether she asks for the repeat, and whether the check-in survives the interruption.
7.evidence: How she handled the question nobody had shown her. This is the criterion the whole block was built for.
7.transition: Move on when she has answered the taxi question.

8.goal: To write down what worked and the one point that becomes the focus of round two.
run: Fill in the board with her: what worked, one point to improve, and — if there was one — the first version of a sentence and a clearer version of it.
One point, not two. It is what she carries into round two.
Ask the question on screen and take the answer as it comes.
Do not add content here.
8.expected: The board filled in, and one point named in words she can act on.
8.support: If she cannot name a difficulty, offer the two you wrote down and let her choose.
8.challenge: Ask her what she would do differently before you say anything.
8.monitoring: Whether the point she names matches the one you observed.
8.evidence: What went into the board. It is what round two is run against.
8.transition: Move on when the board is filled in and the focus is chosen.
exact: Offering the two you observed, if she cannot name one: "Two things I noticed: the greeting, and the request at the end. Which of the two do you want to work on?"

9.goal: The same check-in a second time, with the one focus from the feedback board.
9.interaction: Role-play. You are Emma at the desk again.
run: Copy the point from the feedback board into the focus field on this screen, and explain it to her briefly.
Run the same check-in once more, with that focus and nothing else.
Open Show the phrases only if she needs it.
Write down what changed between the two rounds.
exact: Setting it up: "Same check-in, one thing to watch: " — and read the focus you wrote.
9.expected: The same four moments, with the focus visible in what she does. One improvement is enough.
9.support: Open the phrases and point at the line rather than saying it for her.
9.challenge: Change one detail of the scene — a different date, or a different request.
9.monitoring: Whether the focus shows up in the second round.
9.evidence: What changed between round one and round two. Same task, one focus, one lesson apart.
9.transition: Move on when the second round is done.

10.goal: To close the block out loud, with what exists now that did not exist two weeks ago.
10.interaction: T-S, with self-assessment by the student.
run: Read the list with her and mark what she recognizes. The Portuguese is under each line.
Close the block out loud: four lessons, and a whole check-in in English with a question she was not expecting.
Say the homework out loud, and do not put it on screen: the post-class has the whole check-in to record on her own, one optional writing task and two free resources.
Fill in the block record before you close: did she produce a whole sentence with no model in all four lessons? The planning of the next lessons starts from that answer.
exact: Closing the block: "Two weeks ago you had not said one sentence in English. Today you did a whole check-in, and you handled a question nobody had shown you."
10.expected: Some of the items ticked, and one answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If she ticks nothing, read the list with her and ask which one she could do at a real desk.
10.challenge: Ask which of the four lessons she would repeat, and why.
10.monitoring: Where she puts herself now, against where she put herself in lesson 1.
10.evidence: The block record: whole sentence with no model across the four lessons. It decides the next block.
